item.title: RBI opens special dollar window for oil firms as rupee comes under pressure
item.description: Special window for PSU oil companies from Monday; Forex dealers will not permit users to rebook any foreign exchange derivatives ...
item.dc:creator: Manojit Saha
item.content:encoded: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Saturday announced a host of measures to support the rupee, which is trading close to its all-time low, including a special window to meet the dollar demand of three state-run oil marketing companies (OMCs). The three OMCs are Indian Oil Corporation Ltd (IOC), Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd (HPCL) and Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL). “On the basis of assessment of current market conditions, Reserve Bank of India has decided to open a special window to meet the entire daily dollar requirements of three public sector oil marketing companies,” the RBI said in a press release on Saturday. Under the facility, the RBI will sell dollars to the public sector OMCs through designated banks. The facility will come into effect from October 12, 2026, and will remain in place until further notice, the central bank said. The central bank has also announced regulatory measures for the foreign exchange market and imposed restrictions on the rebooking of cancelled foreign exchange derivative contracts. “Authorised Dealers shall not permit users to rebook any foreign exchange derivative contract involving INR, whether deliverable or non-deliverable, which has been cancelled with any Authorised Dealer after the issuance of the Directions,” the RBI said. Rollover of foreign exchange derivative contracts on maturity will continue to be permitted. The RBI has also reduced the threshold for undertaking foreign exchange derivative transactions without establishing an underlying exposure to $5 million from $100 million. “The corresponding threshold for taking positions in exchange-traded currency derivatives involving INR, without establishing the existence of underlying exposure, has also been reduced from $100 million to $5 million equivalent, across all Recognised Stock Exchanges taken together,” it said. The central bank also introduced a Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve (FERR), requiring forex dealers to maintain a reserve equal to 20 per cent of the notional amount of each eligible derivative transaction involving the rupee. “This FERR shall be applicable for foreign exchange derivative contracts involving INR undertaken to hedge current account exposures where the user purchases foreign currency against the INR,” the RBI said. The central bank said the measures were intended to strengthen market discipline and ensure appropriate risk management in the foreign exchange market, while maintaining an orderly and transparent market environment. The Indian currency has come under pressure since the West Asia conflict began in late February, depreciating 6 per cent. Over the past year, the rupee has depreciated by more than 8 per cent. The central bank has been heavily intervening in the foreign exchange market to curb volatility. India’s foreign exchange reserves declined by about $51.1 billion in the four weeks ended October 2 after touching a record $785.7 billion in the week ended September 4.

item.title: Modi at 25: Small signs, big challenge
item.description: Multiple headwinds make the turbulence Mr Modi is battling as he steps into his 26th year in public office. This has brought the three-point Modi proposition under the greatest pressure since 2014 ...
item.dc:creator: Shekhar Gupta
item.content:encoded: This is the season of looking at Narendra Modi’s 25 years in power and beyond. His followers are celebrating. His Cabinet has passed a resolution praising him. Of course, the critics are out dissecting his quarter-century in public life, not with a scalpel but with a scythe. It’s also the season for people, especially journalists, telling their “when I first met Modi” stories. I’ll hold on to mine for another day. Let’s not risk diluting today’s serious argument. Two weeks ago, we noted that for any incumbent in India, the third year of a term is the toughest. This is when challenges build up, fatigue sets in, aspiring successors sharpen the knives. We also said that the last of these doesn’t apply to Mr Modi. Nobody in his party would even dare to whisper the “S” word. The third year of Mr Modi’s third term, however, is beset with all of the other challenges. His tired and incomplete Cabinet is struggling. His chief ministers — barring Yogi Adityanath, Devendra Fadnavis and Himanta Biswa Sarma — aren’t up to the multiple challenges. Having used the ancient editorial privilege of ‘tabooing’ a word, and listing the cliched “narrative” under it, I then can’t use it. The fact is, this market of popular opinion is rife with competing, contradictory notions. The Modi-BJP story is still the most significant. It just isn’t as dominant as before. Multiple breezes make the turbulence Mr Modi is battling as he steps into his 26th year in public office. This has brought the classical — and so far all-conquering — three-point Modi proposition under the greatest pressure since 2014. The three points are: Hard, Hinduised nationalism; ever-expanding welfare, distributed efficiently, with minimal friction or leakage; and visible construction of physical infrastructure. All of this without significant overhang of corruption. The Modi proposition survives. It’s just that several other factors have now emerged. And we aren’t just talking about the rebellion of an irreverential, ageist, educated and mostly not-impoverished GenZ.  What makes this period of crisis unprecedented in Mr Modi’s prime ministership is the convergence of these factors.. Like the Shakespearean “when sorrows come, they come not single spies, but in battalions.” In isolation, each of these factors may look small. But they become formidable when the big picture comes together. As the great management guru late C K Prahalad used to say: “Weak signals add up to a big change.” He elaborated this in his oft-quoted 1995 paper “Weak Signals Versus Strong Paradigms” (Sage Journals). Prahalad himself summarised it thus: “Taken one at a time, these signals don’t add up to much. But taken together, they present a picture of a country (or industry) in dramatic transformation.” Is this what Mr Modi is confronted with now? Let’s check out some facts. I am reducing these “battalions of sorrows” to a dozen most significant. 1. Dramatic damage to the credibility of the Election Commission of India (ECI), and thereby growing doubts over the integrity of the election process. 2. A growing belief that the top judiciary either doesn’t dare look the executive in the eye, or gives wishy-washy orders. Worse, that it speaks with a forked tongue. Ironically, this view is shared on both sides. 3. A solitary retired civil servant (Subhash Chandra Garg) has triggered a nationwide debate on the credibility of gross domestic product figures. 4. Inflation, as now forecast by the RBI, is set to rise to its highest level in nearly three years, and the rupee is struggling despite a highly successful, if expensive, dollar-deposit scheme. 5. Two of this establishment’s most trusted civil servants, the two Election Commissioners (ECs), protected their own backs by creating a paper trail to record their opposition to the Chief Election Commissioner’s decisions. 6. Ability of the Opposition, especially Rahul Gandhi, to lay siege to the Capital with English TV channels and Hindi newspapers, including the ones ‘most trusted’ by the establishment, giving it prominent airtime. 7. Young people lampooning the Prime Minister with mere feckless pushback from his “Right-wing” supporters, and an overnight phenomenon like CJP setting the agenda, from Neet to the state of government schools. 8. A small ally like Chirag Paswan taking a swipe at Bihar government over law and order. And a way smaller ally, Om Prakash Rajbhar, going public with his purported conversation with the Prime Minister on Uttar Pradesh’s division into multiple states, which Yogi Adityanath firmly opposes. 9. Contrary to the Modi government’s decisive image, we’ve seen festering indecisiveness —whether to press ahead with delimitation, or what to do with a Parliament session that has not been prorogued even two months after its adjournment sine die. To the naked eye, it shows a lack of confidence in marshalling the numbers for constitutional amendments the BJP really wants.  10. Inability, one can also add prolonged hesitation in carrying out a Cabinet reshuffle, or at least filling the vacant slots. There are too many of them, including education. 11. Continued value destruction in the stock market across Mr Modi’s third term, even as all global peers, from the US and Europe to Japan, South Korea, China and even Pakistan, have boomed. The disinclination to acknowledge the challenge is a self-destructive cop-out when millions from the middle class have moved their savings into systematic investment plans and are celebrated by the government for doing so. It also amounts to them having given the fleeing foreign portfolio investors (FPI), a golden handshake. 12. And finally, a global situation for India not seen in decades. Donald Trump has narrowed India’s strategic space in many areas. He’s also challenging our claims to strategic autonomy, with a provocation a day. Beyond Mr Trump, the war in Ukraine, smouldering West Asia, roiled energy markets, and a newly opened strategic-rentier window for Pakistan. All of these have come on top of a deficient monsoon. That’s beyond any government’s control. But these simmering discontents will play out in a below-average farming year. The larger issues, however, are rooted in the three most fundamental factors that have made India cohesive, and stronger over the decades. These are trust in the Constitution and the belief that nobody can take it away, fairness of the top judiciary, and independence of the Election Commission. All three are under strain now. The BJP knows better than its opponents how badly it was damaged in 2024 by rumours fed by just the odd statement from its middling functionaries and the Ayodhya candidate that the party needed 400 seats to change the Constitution. Now most Indians have not read the Constitution, or even the 106 amendments already carried out. But they see the Constitution almost like a deity or a scripture. Fair, secular, a bill of rights they won’t let anybody take away. Constant talk of special Parliament sessions have brought back these suspicions. The Supreme Court has unfortunately built a well-deserved reputation of flip-flops, cynical prevarications, and talking more than writing. This also applies to its treatment of the SIR issue so far. It’s being watched closely now as it battles multiple challenges—from restoring the credibility of the ECI to taking a view on the right to protest in the Capital. And finally, the ECI. Through nearly eight decades, the institution has had good days and bad, and some indifferent ones. It was, however, never as broken as it is now. An ECI caught in an every-man-for-himself trap will struggle to win back popular confidence. It’s a national crisis. These are the challenges Mr Modi needs to address as he steps into his 26th unbroken year in public office. If he doesn’t, or fails to do so, C.K. Prahalad’s small signals could lead to a dramatic crisis over a very painful two and a half years until the summer of 2029.  By special arrangement with ThePrint

item.title: Panama hit by strongest quake in 75 years, 7.7-magnitude tremor strikes
item.description: The earthquake struck Herrera Province more than 193 km southwest of the Panama Canal, with a 6.6-magnitude aftershock and eight others of magnitude 4.8 or higher recorded ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Carolina Pulice and Lauren Rosenthal Panama was hit by its strongest earthquake in more than seven decades on Friday, followed by powerful aftershocks, as President José Raúl Mulino said no deaths had been reported immediately after the quake. The 7.7-magnitude quake struck Herrera Province, more than 120 miles (193 kilometers) southwest of the Panama Canal, according to the US Geological Survey. Economic losses in the region are likely to exceed $1 billion, according to an early USGS estimate. The earthquake was the strongest to hit that part of Panama since at least 1951, according to the US National Earthquake Information Center. It struck at a depth of 12.6 kilometers, the USGS said. A magnitude-6.6 aftershock hit west of the initial quake late Friday afternoon, according to preliminary USGS readings. Another eight aftershocks have been recorded at magnitude 4.8 strength or higher. The first earthquake was caused by a rupture along a major plate boundary on the Ring of Fire, the seismically active zone that encircles the Pacific Ocean. The mechanism resembled a strike-slip event, in which tectonic plates grind past each other horizontally, according to Jonathan Tytell, a geophysicist at the US National Earthquake Information Center. “It was a very messy event, and shallow, which is not good,” Tytell said. “The energy is right there at the surface and it doesn’t really have time or distance to dissipate.” The USGS initially registered an 8.0 magnitude before revising it. Panama’s geological institute reported the quake as a 7.2-magnitude.  Immediately following the quake, the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center said waves of one to three meters (3.3 to 9.8 feet) above tide level were possible along parts of Panama’s coast. As of 2:42 p.m. local time, all warnings had been lifted. The Panama Canal said operations were continuing normally, with emergency protocols activated and technical teams inspecting facilities for possible damage. The quake was felt as far away as several Colombian cities, including Medellín, according to local media. In Panama, people evacuated buildings, businesses, schools and homes across several regions, local newspaper La Prensa said. Panama’s Tocumen International Airport was closed follwoing the quake but was later reopened. Mulino said the government was mobilising personnel, resources and aid for people affected by the quake, and ordered ministries and public agencies to respond immediately and take preventive measures. Emergency officials were expected to hold a news conference to provide an update on the impact.  When touring the affected area Friday, Mulino told reporters that efforts were being made to relocate families away from impacted dwellings. Analysis was also being done about moving patients out of damaged hospitals.Panama’s Finance Minister Felipe Chapman said he contacted the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund and other banks “to obtain the necessary resources to face this crisis.” Corporación Andina de Fomento, known as CAF, one of the contacted institutions, said it was donating $250,000 to Panama for earthquake relief. Mulino thanked CAF for the “promt help.” People stood barefoot or shirtless in the streets as aftershocks continued, said Cibeles De Freitas, a communications representative for the local unit of First Quantum Minerals Ltd. “There’s a lot of fear because we’re not used to earthquakes in Panama,” she said. “We’re OK, just very scared.” First Quantum Minerals said on social media that the infrastructure at Cobre Panama, its partially idled copper mine, located about 140 kilometers north of the epicenter, remained stable and safe following earthquake.  Panama City’s Metro said lines 1 and 2 were temporarily shut down because of the earthquake. Panama’s firefighters said there were no reports of deaths or injuries in the immediate aftermath of the quake. AES Panama, a unit of AES Corp., the country’s top electricity supplier, said through a spokesperson that its hydroelectric, gas-fired and renewable power plants were operational. Activities at the Trans-Panama oil pipeline were continuing normally after the quake, according to a statement from its operator. Friday’s quake was the latest to hit Latin America in recent months. Venezuela was struck by twin earthquakes in late June that killed nearly 6,500 people and caused widespread destruction along its northern coast. In Colombia, an Aug. 10 quake killed more than 330 and prompted an economic emergency as damage was estimated at roughly $10 billion. Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez offered assistance to Panama, as did Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella. “Panama is not alone,” De la Espriella said in a post on X, adding that Colombia was ready to provide whatever assistance was needed. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a social media post he was monitoring the situation, adding that “the State Department is rapidly mobilising resources and personnel to assist.”

item.title: Anthropic's Claude AI carried out unintended actions on US govt websites
item.description: Anthropic disclosed 4 types of unintended AI behaviour, including exploiting software flaws, submitting unauthorised forms and bypassing access restrictions ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Shirin Ghaffary Anthropic PBC said its Claude AI model carried out additional unintended actions on the digital systems of outside organisations, including some US government agencies’ websites, prompting a warning from the Trump administration for artificial intelligence companies to secure their systems. In a report outlining previously undisclosed incidents, Anthropic listed four types of unintended behaviors that the AI has demonstrated, including exploiting basic flaws in software to run commands, submitting forms it should not have and bypassing restrictions to access certain public data. The company said that some of the cases involved websites run by government agencies at the federal, state and local levels, without specifying the agencies. The report did not name the outside entities involved, which Anthropic said was at the request of some of the affected parties.  Anthropic and its rival, OpenAI, have disclosed a spate of incidents in recent months involving their AI models acting in unintended ways, ranging from behaviours like those described in Friday’s report, to hacks of third-party websites. These disclosures have fueled concerns about the security risks of cutting-edge AI. Anthropic said in the report that it sees the behavior as less severe than some other previous incidents involving its AI. “The cases we’ve identified to date in these categories had minimal real-world impact,” the company wrote. In one example of the improper behavior it found, Anthropic said Friday that its Claude Haiku 4.5 model submitted a tip to a local police department about a homicide, stating in the form, “I may have information regarding this case,” and “I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area,” without filling in the site’s name and contact fields. The Philadelphia Police Department disclosed the incident this morning in a press release, the company said. Anthropic also said it briefed the White House on these cases and notified each agency involved. On Friday, Trump administration officials said they were now requiring that AI companies notify affected parties and address security incidents involving their models. “Earlier today, Anthropic contacted the SI Force to disclose the details of various prior incidents that it discovered in late September involving the unauthorised and fraudulent use of government and other systems,” the White House said in a statement from the Super Intelligence Force, a new government unit tasked by President Donald Trump with overseeing AI development and safety.  “The company informed us that these events occurred in the past, the activity has ceased, and there is no ongoing similar activity,” the statement said. Axios reported on the government requirement earlier.  As a result of these uncovered incidents, Anthropic said Friday that it has restricted some types of internet access for its AI models during the testing phase of its training process.
